title: Museveni, Akena killing UPC – Bossa
text: The Observer On May 26, 2016, Dr Olara Otunnu formally resigned as president of the Uganda People’s Congress (UPC) and handed the reins to his deputy Joseph Bossa. This plunged the party into a leadership fight pitting Otunnu and Bossa, on the one side, against the James Akena-led faction. In a ruling this month, deputy Chief Justice Steven Kavuma ordered Bossa and his allies (Prof Edward Kakonge and Isha Otto) not to interfere with how Akena and his cabinet run the party. He further ordered that an order made by High court judge, Yasin Nyanzi, in 2015 declaring that Akena was illegally elected should not to be executed until the main application is heard. Days before the ruling, Bossa, a former financial lawyer with Bank of Uganda, spoke to Abubaker Mayemba about the wrangles in his party. Excerpts: What do you make of Akena’s recent assertion that he is running a functioning party? A functioning headquarters? He did it through violence because he got goons who threw out the true leadership of UPC and the entire secretariat [in 2015]. He occupied it and continues to do so with the support of the Uganda police. If you are not a UPC president and you are occupying the party’s headquarters, does that make it a functioning headquarters? You have thrown out the legitimate leadership; so, whatever you are doing there is illegal. This man [Akena] has the capacity to tell lies without any shame. One thing I admire about Akena is his capacity to ignore facts and believe facts of his own creation. The name for that in psychological medicine is, psychotic, a person who lives in a world of his own imaginations. He will even think he is the president of Uganda. Before party elections last year, Otunnu and Akena had ironed out their differences. Akena was even allowed to pick nomination forms after the deadline passed. What happened? We thought he was genuinely interested in seeking the presidency of UPC in a straightforward manner. Mr Otunnu thought that closing him out because the deadline had passed would make him go around the world claiming he had been discriminated against. Of course, he would never have mentioned that the deadline for picking papers had passed. He would simply tell the world he was disqualified because Otunnu discriminates against him. So, Otunnu said, “okay, even though I strongly believe that Akena is not interested in the UPC leadership perse, he is a mole, let him contest and the people decide.” When we had district conferences, by 3:00 o’clock he had invaded the headquarters and held hostage the secretariat and electoral commission staff who were waiting for results from the districts. He and his group were, instead, giving them results. He later decided before arrival of the full results, that since he had won in 65 districts, he had won the election. He came back and confronted the electoral commission and said; “in view of the fact that we have got 65 districts, it’s no longer mathematically-possible for other candidates to get the one-third support; so, I should go to the delegates’ conference. So, only I can go and I’m president-elect.” It was Akena deciding. How did he do that yet the EC had powers to say he was not party president yet? It was physical. They [EC] were virtually, at gunpoint. They had been surrounded; so, out of five commissioners, I think two or three, but excluding the chairman, signed, declaring that he [Akena] was president-elect. We don’t even have that concept in our party constitution. On Monday those of us who had been presidential aspirants filed our complaints about the electoral process with the Electoral Review Board (ERB). We told them that in some of the districts, none of our members had participated in the conferences and in some areas no election took place. In Kampala, my agent told me that he saw non-party members come to vote, people who couldn’t identify themselves on the voting list. Mr Otunnu, the party president then, said that ‘okay let’s meet on Friday June 5 with the EC and ERB members and all candidates and see what we can do.’ We tendered in our complaints. All candidates were asked to step out so that the two organs make decisions. When they were still deliberating, Akena and group stormed the boardroom in huge numbers and dragged the EC members to the press room with cameras flashing and instructed them to declare Akena president. Otunnu declined. He said if they wanted to kill him, they were free to do so but he refused to declare Akena party president. That is when he [Otunnu] walked out, that’s when you saw pictures of people calling him a rat, a rat is running out and all that. From that time, they occupied the headquarters of UPC. Akena says the ERB was a tool created by Otunnu to push his agenda and he couldn’t accept its decision. The Election Review Board never functioned. It did not make a single pronouncement. It was supposed to hear complaints but he didn’t allow it. You said elections were not conducted and there were no people in some places. Don’t you blame that on your party structure? As vice president, do you think you built any party grassroots structures? Grassroots are a difficult issue because of two reasons. In December 2014, when we were trying to prepare for the March 2015 delegates’ conference to elect a new party president, Fred Ebil went to court and obtained an injunction against any party activity. So, we couldn’t even hold elections. But in early 2013, we got some money from our supporters. It was Shs 200m and half of it was to buy furniture and the rest to facilitate elections for new structures. A section of members got hold of the money and started holding fake seminars and some badly- organised elections. In the end, all the money got finished. We went into that election deeply hobbled because we were to meet this deadline of a new leadership. When the date expired, they went to court and said Otunnu’s term had expired, so there was no president. And that’s when Justice Stephen Musota said the party leader remains until after fresh elections.[The judge ruled that there was already an on-going election road map and that Article 26(1) of the party constitution stipulates it clearly that a person shall continue holding office until new elections are held]. When the ruling was issued, that’s when Akena rushed to pick papers. When court said Otunnu still had powers, Akena knew that he would be left out, that’s when he pressured Otunnu to allow him pick nomination papers. When you say the leadership is to blame for not conducting elections, you are wrong. As given in the background, failure of the regime to conduct elections can be pinned on the stealing of money and the court injunction prohibiting party activities. Akena called a consultative meeting of UPC members in Lugogo. When they convened, within five minutes they passed a decision to constitute themselves into a delegates’ conference. Were these people senior members? We don’t know, but some were not. In any case, it wasn’t an organ of UPC and we don’t know in what capacity they were in there. But in any case, the point was that whether they are senior party members or not, they couldn’t convert a consultative meeting into a delegates’ conference. A delegates’ conference, according to our constitution, can only be convened by the party president not any member, be it senior. After that, they went on to make a resolution saying Akena has been elected president. That’s when I went to court asking whether it was true that the electoral commission and UPC [had] declared Akena president. And court agreed with me that whatever document had been signed declaring Akena president was null and void. Akena says he has appealed but when you appeal, the decision of the lower court remains in force until the higher court has reversed it. He will now say he went to the Court of Appeal and court ruled that the status quo remains. Whatever interpretation you may want to put on that ruling, the status quo is: Justice Nyanzi said he is not president. By February 15, 2016, the UPC bank account had already been frozen not on my own initiative but the bank’s. They wrote saying that because the leadership of the party was in dispute; it [bank] had decided to freeze the party’s account. Now Akena says I’m blocking party activities because I went to court and froze the account. That is misinformation. I did not. It was the bank, on its own, which said that it was hard to know who should run the account; so, it blocked it. Akena maintains that because you people blocked the account, the party does not have funds to run its activities. First of all, he is not the president. He should not run the party. Secondly, neither I nor Otunnu ordered that. When we got the Justice Nyanzi order, we went to the bank, saying Akena had no mandate to run the account. We asked them to restore the signatories but the bank decided that neither we nor they[Akena] would be allowed to operate the account. That’s why they froze it. We don’t have access to the account. I went to court to dispute Akena’s presidency and not to block the accounts. 2021 is getting closer and you are still fighting; doesn’t that affect you? It does concern me very much. But for many years, Otunnu was telling the world, diplomatically, that Akena was a mole in UPC, working closely with NRM. He claims he is working with him [President Museveni] to build a better Uganda. We work with NRM after being sanctioned by the party organs. But when you go on your own, after grabbing power, and begin working with Museveni, you are doing so outside the party’s constitution. If they say you have been cooperating as a mole, then their argument is right. For instance, in April 2011 after the general elections, we went to Mukono and the National Council (NC) passed a decision authorising the cabinet to coordinate with any individual or democracy-seeking organisation for the betterment of the country. Even if UPC worked with FDC, DP, CP and Jeema, then that partnership was in line with the mandate given by the NC. How is Akena’s cooperation with NRM affecting the party? Museveni and NRM are using Akena to destabilise the party. They occupy party headquarters; they disrupt our meetings. As the true leadership of the party, we had organised a council meeting of the NC to map the way forward for the party. Akena, using the police, stormed the meeting and disrupted us. The chief organisers like Peter Walubiri and Isha Otto Amizza were locked up in Kireka cells for two days. As the “true leaders of UPC”, have you tried to engage the police? Too much, we complained to the Central police station, Kampala, and said ‘someone is occupying our premises’. They refused to cooperate with us. Otunnu at some moment met with the Inspector General of Police Kale Kayihura and explained the situation to him. He pretended he was not aware and asked Otunnu to write to him but when Otunnu wrote, he got no reply. The Milton Obote Foundation (MOF), the owners of Uganda House, went to CPS and said an unrecognised group has thrown out their clients and refused to leave the premises, the police did nothing. MOF even opened a criminal trespass case against the Akena faction, the director of public prosecutions (DPP) took it up but later gave it up. Not only we as leaders of UPC but even the owners of Uganda House have engaged police and went to court. NRM through police have frustrated all our efforts. They say you are being used by MOF, that during your tenure in office, you failed to monitor MOF’s spending. He should not mix issues. The accountability between UPC and MOF, that has nothing to do with the leadership of UPC. It has nothing to do with the succession in UPC. Whether we did or did not, has nothing to do with Akena being the UPC president now. We are saying ‘Akena, you should have allowed the election to take its course. You disrupted it by making yourself president of UPC and you should have followed the party constitution. We don’t care who you are and where you are from. We are just saying that’s not the way leadership of UPC is determined.’ Courts have said he didn’t follow the party constitution, don’t colour that with anything else. Don’t say we are fighting him, we are fighting the process. How are preparations to replace Otunnu progressing? I have gone very far with the elections. As soon as I was elected, I set up a committee to organise elections. One thing they have started with is to organise a national council meeting [due soon]. The NC will give us guidance on how and when to hold a delegates’ conference to elect a party president. The NC meeting will determine for us who qualifies to stand for president and how the election will run. What have you achieved so far as party president? I have survived. The party is still here. My main aim at the end of the day is to ensure that before the six months I was given expire, the party would have elected a new president. Are you going to contest? As far as I am concerned, the party constitution doesn’t bar me. We are going to pass new rules that if the national council meeting decides that I shouldn’t run, even if I wish, that would be it. The NC will determine who is eligible to stand. Before Christmas this year, UPC will have elected a new president. Won’t the Akena faction disrupt the process? If Akena, the NRM and police decide to disrupt the process, let the blood be upon them. Let them tell the world why they did it. But that should not be the reason for failure, on our part, to try. Where are your offices and how do you handle the finances now that Akena’s faction occupies Uganda House? We have offices in Mabirizi plaza on Kampala road. That is where we are operating from. But I have been telling members that UPC is not about the physical place, the 6th floor of Uganda House is not UPC. In fact, since its inception, UPC moved into Uganda House in 1980 but it remained a political force. UPC has even operated outside Uganda, when Milton Obote was in Tanzania. Don’t put too much emphasis on the physical floor at Uganda House. We are operating minimally, the little money that we have has been frozen by the bank. abumay1988@gmail.com Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. Link Copy link

title: MPs: Govt cheated on properties abroad
text: The Observer MPs have said that all Ugandan properties abroad should be managed by the country’s foreign missions and not a private company; Uganda Property Holdings Limited (UPHL). This recommendation is aimed to reduce losses and is part of a report by the parliamentary committee on Foreign Affairs unveiled last week. “Parliament should investigate the management of UPHL in relation to the management of assets and revenue collection,” said Rose Mutonyi, the committee chairperson. Much of the money collected by UPHL is spent on operational costs and the report found that only Shs 150m of the Shs 6.7bn collected in the financial year 2015/16 was remitted to government. “The committee was informed by the management of UPHL in Mombasa that in the financial year 2015/16, only Shs 6.7bn was generated from 22 properties plus two from London, of which Shs 4.3bn was spent on operational costs and a further Shs2.2bn reinvested, leaving Shs150m as the net profit to be shared by stakeholders,” reads the report. “And yet a single building, Uganda House in Nairobi, in its dilapidated form fetched Shs1.06bn in remittances to the consolidated fund in 2015/16. The government of Uganda is, therefore, getting a raw deal from UPHL,” the report says. The report, which will be debated after MPs return from recess on December 20, 2016, also found that Ugandan missions in Khartoum, Abuja and Cairo did not have substantive heads of mission. According to the committee, the host countries may view this as a lack of commitment by Uganda to maintain diplomatic relations. The committee urged the ministry of Foreign Affairs to conduct a human resource audit of all missions and engage the ministries of public service and finance on a phased approach to filling the existing gaps. The committee also noted that Uganda risks losing prime land in Nigeria and Addis Ababa, Ethiopia due to failure to develop it. A 2.5 acre piece of land in Nigeria may be repossessed due to failure by government to develop it while another 2.5 acre piece of land fully paid by government in Adis Ababa has been encroached upon by a private developer who has since fenced it off. namuloki16@gmail.com Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. title: Court sets Dec 20 for Kamoga bail hearing
text: The Observer International Crimes division of the High court (ICD) Justice Duncan Gaswaga will tomorrow hear the bail application of Muslim clerics accused of terrorism, murder and attempted murder. Sheikhs Muhammad Yunus Kamoga, Siraj Kawooya, Sekayanja Abdulsalaam alias Kassim Mulumba, Sematimba Abdulhamid Mubiru, Rashid Jingo, Twaha Sekitto, Yusuf Kakande alias Abdallah, Murta Mudde Bukenya, Fahad Kalungi, Hamuza Kasirye and Musa Issa Mubiru have applied for bail. The clerics are charged with the murder of Sheikhs Mustapha Bahiga in 2014 and Ibrahim Hassan Kirya in 2015. They also face charges of attempted murder of Prince Kassim Nakibinge, the titular head of the Muslim community in Uganda, Sheikh Haruna Jemba, Najib Ssonko and Mahmood Kibaate. The suspects have so far spent two years in Luzira prison since their arrest in January 2015. Prosecution, led by principal state attorneys Lino Anguzu and Thomas Jatiko, has presented 22 witnesses in court presided over by Justices Ezekiel Muhanguzi, Percy Tuhaise and Jane Kiggundu. III HEALTH In his affidavit supporting the bail application, Kamoga cites his deteriorating health. Kamoga, the head of the Tabliq community in Uganda, also says he is of advanced age [62 years] and grave ailments such as peptic ulcers, asthma and hypertension have taken a toll on his health. Although the trial started on October 17, 2016, it has been halted by court because government says it doesn’t have funds to sustain it. That, he said, has denied him a speedy and fair trial. “That I’m a well-known Muslim leader and religious cleric with interest in having the matter heard and concluded and as such, I will not abscond from court,” Kamoga says. “That my liberation will not affect the prosecution case in any way since investigations are complete and the evidence is already gathered and I don’t know any of the state witnesses,” he says. Through law firms led by Muwema and company advocates, Kamoga says his family has suffered as a result of his endless detention. “That I’m a sole breadwinner of my family, which is currently suffering in my absentia,” he says, adding, “my businesses which I used to run have since collapsed due to my incarceration.” FAHAD KALUNGI In his affidavit supporting his bail application, Fahad Kalungi says, “…I’m a law-abiding citizen, in fact as chairman of Energy Centre Tenants and Traders Association, I worked closely and aided police to stop lawlessness in that business area.” Kalungi also accuses prosecution lawyers of undermining his defence through amending the charge sheet endlessly. When he was arraigned before the Nakawa chief magistrate’s court on January 22, 2015, Kalungi says he was charged with crimes against humanity, terrorism, murder and attempted murder. “That on February 10, 2015 the charges against me and others were amended to one count of aiding or rendering support to ADF and associates to be used in acts of terrorism and we were committed to the High court [International Crimes division],” he says. “That the charges were again amended several times before the commencement of the trial.” Meanwhile, other suspects; George William Iga, Amir Kinene and Hakim Kinene Muswaswa, who are represented by MacDosman Kabega, didn’t apply for bail. The substantive trial of Kamoga and his co-accused was adjourned to January 11, 2017. dkiyonga@observer.ug Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. Link Copy link

title: MP Nandala-Mafabi faults Utl on Shs 670bn debts
text: The Observer Budadiri West MP Nathan Nandala-Mafabi has lashed out at Uganda Telecom Limited (Utl) for mismanagement. Mafabi made these revelations last week while appearing before a probe committee that is investigating the financial malaise in the telecom company. This, he said, includes irregular transactions and sale of some of its properties and land, staff harassment and fraud. Government owns a 31 per cent stake in Utl while Libya African Portfolio Green owns 69 per cent shares. The committee, chaired by Okin Ojara, comprises Michael Tusiime, William Nzoghu, Paula Turyahikayo, Lillian Nakate and Thomas Tayebwa. Mafabi further stated that Utl is “bleeding financially in local and foreign debts to a tune of Shs 670 billion, with no audit done for the last four years.” He said without audits of company accounts and assets, it took long to detect fraud that went on for years where petty cash to the tune of more than Shs 1.5 billion also vanished. He also claimed that Utl’s recently-authorized installation of a superfast high capacity internet link has the ability to tap President Museveni’s phone calls. “It should be noted that such capacity would enable the user with system passwords to do anything with the Utl network including tapping the calls of His Excellency the president and other security agencies,” Mafabi said. Mafabi told the MPs that there is need for Utl managing director, Mark Shoebridge, to explain what the superfast connection, whose installation he authorized, is being used for. The MP claimed Utl management is using bank access rights of former staff to make payments, some of which are highly-questionable. “For instance on December 6, 2016, Shs 50m was paid to URA purportedly signed by John Sendikaddiwa, almost a month after he left the company,” Mafabi told the committee. Last month, parliament imposed a travel ban on Utl’s top management pending investigations but the committee noted that some of the banned managers continue to travel out of the country. According Mafabi, since he exposed the mismanagement of Utl, Shoebridge has fired those he believes are responsible for leaking the information. “Some of the staff who have left include John Sendikaddiwa, Charles Wanume, John Magala and Godfrey Kisekka (who was the acting MD before Shoebridge took over),” Mafabi said. “It is therefore my recommendation that the acts going on in Utl, including the wanton victimization of staff, is stopped with immediate effect.” The committee said the top managers who include Shoebridge, company secretary David Nambale, James Wilde, the chief finance officer; Emmanuel Kasule, the chief human resource officer and Ameer Kamal Arif, the chief commercial officer, be investigated. namuloki16@gmail.com Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. title: Rugunda speaks on Makerere, fighting ministers
text: The Observer Two years since he replaced Amama Mbabazi as prime minister in September 2014, DR RUHAKANA RUGUNDA talks to Sadab Kitatta Kaaya, offering a measured assessment of his own tenure as leader of government business in parliament. Below are excerpts: It is seven months since the new government was inaugurated, how do you rate your cabinet? Since May, government has worked well; it has energetically embarked on a number of projects, basically consolidation and completion of projects that were underway especially in the infrastructure area. It has handled issues of Operation Wealth Creation to ensure that there is increased production in agriculture, leading to increased incomes for the population. It has embarked on special programs for the women, youths, to ensure that they have projects, jobs and increased income. Recently we have had some challenges in the area of food security [but] government has mobilized politically and organized material resources so that we can feed our people. We have done a lot in the region especially with our regional interactions with our neighbours, especially on [the situation in South Sudan]. We have had interactions with our Kenyan neighbours on our regional projects and the northern corridor programs going on, [and] preparations continue for the Standard Gauge Railway. We have looked at a number of challenges in the education sector, which we are dealing with, Makerere [University] is a case in point and [some] other universities. So, in a nutshell, government is on course, it is doing what it promised the nation. Talking about the food security problem, critics say the food relief you are sending to the famine-hit districts is too little. Did you underestimate the problem? It is true that we have sent out food relief [and] we are fully aware that it cannot be enough. The focus, however, has been to concentrate on the very badly-hit, the elderly, [expectant] mothers and the sick, especially those on treatment. Could that be the reason why government is now considering suspending some infrastructural development projects and divert the money to buying food? We will do whatever we can to make sure that the people of Uganda are protected from famine brought on by the drought. If it becomes necessary, yes, government is very ready to reconsider; to review the budget in order to ensure that there is provision for the critically- required food to save lives. Public universities have been striking; Makerere is now closed; are the university problems too complex for government to fix? First of all, most of the universities in the country are stable. They are working, and working well. It is true there has been quite a bit of hassling, quite a number of strikes at Makerere but Makerere is a bit of an exception and should not be used as a standard reflection of what is happening in universities in the country. There are a few others like Kabale, which is a new public university [which] has had a few challenges but really all universities are settled, teaching and doing well. In case issues come up, government through the ministry of education addresses them. Why does government have to wait for the problems to go out of hand? Government does not wait; on the contrary, government tackles some of these issues and sometimes when you hear of a strike, it is more often a reflection of reaching a point of divergence or disagreement between government and some of the people involved. It is not that government has been waiting, government is continuing, and has been addressing some of these issues… That is why President Museveni established a visitation committee for Makerere University to be able to address the fundamental issues holistically. Is there hope that Makerere University will be opened soon? There is no doubt about that. Every one of us wants Makerere University to be opened, and soon. However, certain critical, fundamental issues that have been causing these regular strikes must be addressed. What are the issues? Let’s leave that for the visitation committee. You have been holding the office of prime minister for more than two years now, how have you found it? First of all, it has given me an opportunity to serve the country in a more responsible position. Definitely, I must thank the president for the confidence he entrusted in me. I’m doing what I can to serve both Parliament and the government. A prime minister is a team leader, and so, I serve with my comrades, my political colleagues – the ministers. We work as a team, where one is not available, the other one handles, and I think, our working as a team is very promising. But we see fights between some cabinet members, for example Hon Aidah Nantaba (state for ICT) against Persis Namuganza (state for Lands); the other day your finance minister and his junior made separate appointments for the same position. How are you dealing with these conflicts? I must say that the cabinet we have today is a very cohesive cabinet and work is going on very well. Occasionally, when you have a family, there may be a difference of opinion and quite often, the media cherishes and thrives on such difference of opinion. When such an issue comes up; the individual ministers concerned sort it out, and if necessary, the prime minister comes in or the government chief whip. All in all, the issues are under control. A senior minister making an appointment and his junior also making another does not reflect a lot of cohesion… There is nothing lacking, and the ministers have already sorted out those issues. It is seven months into the term of the 10th Parliament but we are not seeing much business coming to Parliament from the executive. Instead, we are seeing private members’ bills. What’s lacking? There is plenty of business from government in Parliament and there are many bills being considered by the various committees of Parliament. There are also bills that we had saved even from the last Parliament, those are also being considered. A full list of bills was submitted at the beginning of the 10th Parliament, different ministries are at different stages of submitting them [the bills]. Some have already been read for the first time, [and] gone to the committees and we are waiting for them to be read for the second time. Yes there are some bills, but some MPs say there should be much more. Well, the Leader of government business [in Parliament] has a different view. When you look at the order paper, you’ll find that there is a lot of pending business. Secondly, we encourage MPs to be at liberty to initiate private members’ bills. Some of them are under consideration, [and] when some come, we liaise with [the sponsors] and sometimes government takes on some of these bills. It is a question of teamwork, [between] government and members of the backbench. You yourself have been accused of missing many parliamentary sittings – maybe what you never miss is the prime minister’s question time! First of all, that is false. I am in the House not just only for the prime minister’s question time. But it is also true that my brother, the 1st deputy prime minister and deputy leader of government business in parliament, Gen Moses Ali, when he is there, I don’t need to be there, I attend to other government responsibilities. When Rt Hon Moses is there, it means that I am also there, and even the Government Chief Whip Hon Ruth Nankabirwa. When she is there, government is [represented]. The critical point is, is there adequate representation of the government? The answer is yes. It doesn’t have to be the person of the prime minister. And, by the way, [government is also represented] by the presence of ministers. Because of the heavy schedule, sometimes one is busy with other things; that is why you and I are having this interview at 8:15pm. It is not because Rugunda planned this in order to impress Kitatta. It is because the schedule of work is heavy and one doesn’t have to be in Parliament when there is adequate representation. There are times when the House has had to be adjourned because there are no ministers to respond to issues raised. That is just a question of coordination, sometimes, ministers may not be adequately informed; there may be some misinformation. If the minister knows that he or she is on the order paper, they will come, but sometimes that information is missing. Can you elaborate on what you mean by misinformation? The order paper may come out late morning or early afternoon. So, sometimes the information on what is on the order paper may not be available to the ministers [in time] and so, the minister may not realize that he or she would be required to be in the House to answer certain questions. But the main point is to encourage the ministers to ensure that they are available but they have very many other demands. Our understanding and our guidance is that if a minister is not in the House, then another colleague must stand in. The minister must [alert] a colleague to stand in for him or her, or to send the minister of state. Do you then think that the leadership at Parliament should change the way they operate? The order paper coming earlier would be perfectly okay. Or even for that matter, the order paper [should be able] to indicate the following day’s business. Our order paper indicates the day’s business and a notice of business to follow. That partly covers it, [and] one can say that we have indeed, and we shall continue to encourage ministers to be in Parliament, but it will have to be reconciled with other schedules. How does it feel serving a government with high corruption ratings? In my assessment, I am aware that there is some corruption in the government, and government is dealing with it head-on. That is why we have in place the auditor general to help government in exposing the problem. That is why we have the IGG [Inspector General of Government] to dig out any corruption so that government deals with it. That’s why we have the CID [Criminal Investigations Directorate of the police] to deal with the investigations so that the necessary legal measures can be taken. That’s why we have the DPP [Directorate of Public Prosecutions] to prosecute corruption cases; that is why we have the Anti-Corruption court to deal with the problem straight on. All in all, yes, there is corruption but government has taken extraordinary steps to deal with it and I am sure, we have the upper hand in the fight against corruption. What are the extraordinary steps, because there are cases of corrupt officials in the auditor general’s reports not being given due attention. I would be interested in hearing from my son Kitatta in relation to who is corrupt and has been shielded. Can you educate me? Have you not heard people being prosecuted because of the auditor general’s revelation or CID and IGG? There is no small or big fish. So long as you are accused, the law will take its course, and as you are very well aware, both the big and small [fish] have appeared in courts of law. That will, indeed, be the order of business. Is government, therefore, ashamed of the rampant corruption? Government is very proud that it is facing corruption head-on… We are dealing with it with no compromise, and we’ll intensify our efforts to make sure that we defeat this monster but we would like the public not to be shy but to come out and give us information so that we can deal with this scourge of corruption. sadabkk@observer.ug Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. title: Lukwago, Kamya set to talk
text: The Observer After six months in which Kampala lord mayor Lukwago’s council made law and minister Beti Kamya did what she wanted, the two leaders want to talk peace, and make the city work, SIRAJE LUBWAMA reports. In an unintended New Year gift to a city they have been fighting over, Kampala’s top political rivals say they are now ready to work together. Speaking to The Observer last week, lord mayor Erias Lukwago said he was tired or wars, while Kampala minister Beti Kamya promised to hunt down Lukwago and talk. Lukwago first announced his engagement strategy during Thursday’s year-ending Kampala Capital City Authority, (KCCA) meeting at City Hall. Calling for a “united team”, Lukwago lamented both minister Kamya and District Land Board chairman Yusuf Nsibambi had skipped the meeting, citing other commitments. Since city councillors took oath in June, Kamya has not attended a single KCCA sitting. Lukwago once said that Kamya was sent by President Museveni to fight the lord mayor. Lukwago was elected with a landslide, the voters defying President Museveni’s spirited campaign for ‘anyone but Lukwago’. Meanwhile, Council has sat and passed resolutions, which Kamya has ignored or contradicted – something Lukwago says hurts him. In November, lord councillors resolved not to force vendors and hawkers off the city streets, until a place was found to relocate them to. But Kamya got police and other law enforcement agencies to evict the vendors. “I will not call any other authority meeting until this matter [of reconciling with Kamya] is put to rest,” Lukwago told councillors. “I would like this to happen not later than 15th January 2016 because I want a united team that would deliver services to Kampala dwellers better. I, therefore, call upon my sister, the honourable minister, and the technical staff to join the political team in developing the city.” Earlier in the meeting, councilor Faridah Nakabugo called for a resolution advising Kamya to resign or ask the appointing authority to sack her. This was rejected, with one division mayor saying council had no basis to force the minister to attend its meeting. Rooted in mutual political suspicion, the conflict between Lukwago and Kamya has often manifested in different interpretations of the KCCA Act. In June, Lukwago told the parliamentary committee on Presidential Affairs that according to the KCCA Act, Kamya has no powers to implement council policies. Rejecting this, Kamya said the law empowered her to implement policies and hold the lord mayor accountable to her and the authority. Last week, council resolved that if Kamya accepted to attend a peace-making council meeting, Lukwago would let deputy lord mayor Sarah Kanyike chair it. Kamya’s personal assistant, Lt Francis Matovu, told us at the weekend that the minister was not to blame for skipping KCCA meetings. He said Kamya chose to be represented by one of her personal assistants, Hassan Kasibante, because when she invites the lord mayor for meetings, Lukwago sends his deputy Sarah Kanyike. “Before the minister swore in, she called Lukwago for a talk, he did not honour it,” Matovu said. “She invited him for several functions, including the introduction ceremony of her daughter, which he promised to attend but instead sent his deputy. She came to the mayor’s parlor but instead Lukwago sent his deputy to the meeting attended by division mayors.” TIME FOR PEACE Interviewed for a comment on Saturday, minister Kamya promised to talk to Lukwago. “As I talk now, I am at a church function in Lubaga division. Today [Saturday] morning, I rang the lord mayor inviting him to come and welcome the Chief justice Bart Katureebe at this function; he has not honoured the invitation despite the chief justice not being a politician,” Kamya said. “As a Protestant and a born-again, I am more than willing to meet Lukwago at any time anywhere. Even if he dodges this time, I will hunt for him wherever he will be. …Better late than never.” Contacted separately on Saturday, Lukwago told The Observer: “It is only last Thursday that she [Kamya] said she was attending another important event but I am now tired of fighting wars. I want next year to be a year of working rather than arguing with people I should be working closely with. I want her [Kamya] to choose a day of her choice when she is free to have a reconciliatory meeting.” Deputy Mayor Kanyike told us on Saturday that councillors had chosen her and Andrew Kitaka, the acting deputy executive director of KCCA, to contact Kamya. “If the minister accepts to meet me and Kitaka, we shall hopefully make her choose a day for a reconciliation meeting,” Kanyike said. “Thereafter, we shall agree with her on the best day for the authority meeting she wishes to attend”. slubwama@observer.ug Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. title: Man held over injecting two nephews with HIV+ blood
text: The Observer Police in Kabale is holding a twenty-two-year-old man for allegedly injecting his two nephews with blood infected with HIV/Aids. The suspect, Bosco Ngusi, a resident of Hakabungo cell in Mukaranje ward, Katuna town council is said to have injected the two kids on December 12. Katuna town council LC III chairperson, Nelson Nshangabashaija, says Ngusi used a syringe to draw infected blood from his body before injecting it into the two children – all aged four. Nshangabashaija says that the suspect has been staying with his grandmother and is believed to have acquired the virus from his late parents. Elly Maate, the police spokesperson for Kigezi region says that the suspect was arrested on Saturday from his hideout in Katuna town council. He is being detained at Kabale central police station. “He is said to have spread the contagious disease, HIV/Aids to [the] kids. He used a syringe. He got blood from himself and injected the two kids on their buttocks. Actually, this is the worst scandal of the season the person being so malicious to his own sister’s innocent kids. Intentional transmission of infectious disease to poor innocent kids! We have him and after investigations, he must be aligned in court because such people living in our communities are very dangerous and deadly,” Maate said. In January 2014, Rosemary Namubiru, a 65-year-old nurse at Victoria Medical Centre in Kampala was arrested for allegedly injecting a two-year-old baby with blood infected with HIV/Aids. title: Couple sues Marie Stopes over unplanned child
text: The Observer A couple has sued Marie Stopes-Uganda, an organisation that, according to its mission allows women have children by choice, not by chance, for giving them false assurance on birth control. Jackson and Mary Okiring filed the suit before the High court in Kampala. They say that they were advised by Marie Stopes, to undergo a bilateral tubal litigation, a surgical procedure that involves blocking the fallopian tubes to prevent the ovum from being fertilized. The procedure, considered a permanent form of birth control, is be done by cutting, burning or removing sections of the fallopian tubes. On the basis that they already had a sizeable number of children and faced financial constraints, the couple took the advice of the health service provider and underwent the procedure with an assurance that Mary would never conceive again. However, the ‘distressed’ couple says in early 2016, they were shocked to learn that Mary was pregnant. The couple says it has so far incurred a cost of Shs 2.5 million as expenses of raising the unplanned child and that they have been subjected to stress and pain resulting from the negligence and false assurances. They now want court to order Marie Stopes to compensate them with the Shs 2.5 million that they have so far spent and take over the responsibility of raising the child in question. Marie Stopes Uganda is part of the Marie Stopes international non-governmental organisation providing contraception and safe abortion service in 37 countries around the world. title: Two banks probed over Shs 8bn fraud, murder of Eritrean
text: The Observer Police is investigating two banks in Kampala in connection with a syndicate that plotted to swindle 2 million Euros (about Shs 8 billion) from an Eritrean national. Police spokesperson Andrew Felix Kaweesi says that the Eritrean, Daniel Weldo, 32, had moved to Kampala because of the volatile situation in South Sudan, where he was running businesses. Weldo had saved up to 2 million Euros on an account in one of the Ugandan banks. However, Kaweesi adds, his encounter with an organized syndicate put his life in danger. He was reported missing on October 27. Reports indicated that he had been kidnapped by unknown persons. His body was found dumped in a farm near Busia district, Kenya over the weekend. “Since October police mounted serious overt and covert operations to recover him alive. Unfortunately that wasn’t the case. When he was kidnapped, he was taken and murdered in Kenya, in the Busia district of Kenya. The body was dumped in a swamp. And when we arrested one of the suspects he led us to where the body had been dumped. We have so far arrested three people.” Kaweesi says that prior investigations have unveiled a syndicate involving two banks and three people who could have connived to eliminate the businessman in order to get hold of his savings. Although he did not name the banks, Kaweesi named the suspected individual accomplices as UPDF Captain Hakeem Mangeni, the mastermind of the plot; Ben Lumu and Lucy Katuramu. According to Kaweesi, although the core business between the three suspects is not known, preliminary investigations indicate that Weldo contacted them in his search for a Germany visa. He added that the trio had accomplices in the banks with whom they worked in the hope that there will be no claimant to the money once the owner is eliminated. Kaweesi says it is not the first time; there is an attempt on the life and finances of a foreigner by the two banks and suspects. Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. Link Copy link

title: FIFA fines Uganda Shs 17m, Burundi Shs 55m
text: The Observer World football governing body, FIFA has sanctioned several East African states including Uganda for various incidents during the 2018 FIFA World Cup qualifiers. In a circular released on Monday, by the Federation of International Football Associations disciplinary committee said Ugandan fans were seated in an ‘improper place’ during the game with Togo at the Mandela national stadium, Namboole on November 15, 2015. The Ugandan federation has received a warning and has been asked to pay a fine of Shs 17,502,155 (5,000 Swiss Francs). Federation of Uganda Football Associations (Fufa) deputy CEO Humphrey Mandu said they are yet to receive the communication. Burundi who will pay Shs 35,004,306 (10,000 Swiss Francs) for infringement of media and marketing regulations when they hosted Ivory Coast and another Shs 20,957,037 (6,000 Swiss Francs) for fielding an ineligible player (Gael Bigirimana) in the away game to the same team. Kenya were also fined Shs 35,004,306 (10,000 Swiss Francs) for the late arrival of their team in Cape Verde which resulted to a late kick-off in the 2018 World Cup qualifier on November 13, 2015. South Sudan has also fined 7,500 Swiss Francs for a direct red card by Aluck Mabior in the game against Mauritania. Many other nations around the world including England, Chile and China among others were also fined for incidents during the World Cup qualifier and international friendlies. title: Residents protest against delayed Unra pay
text: The Observer Residents of Kitgum and Pader districts have held a peaceful demonstration to protest delayed compensation by Uganda National Roads Authority (Unra). More than 50 people from Pader and Kitgum took to the streets on Monday to express their dissatisfaction with Unra. Last month, residents affected by the Gulu-Acholibur-Musingo road works convened a meeting at Acholibur in Pader district in the presence of Unra engineers and district officials. They gave the authority a two week’s ultimatum to respond to their grievances. However, Unra didn’t respond to the concerns, prompting residents to storm the streets. Alfred Okwera from Labongo-Layamo sub-county blames Katuramu and Company for continuing to issue the affected persons with payment vouchers for undervalued property despite their repeated complaints. John Ocan, 78, says he has failed to maintain his home after the only commercial house from which he earned Shs 1.7m each month was demolished to pave way for the road works. Charles Nyeko, the chairperson of the affected persons, said this was the last time they would be demonstrating peacefully. He cautions Unra to comply with their concerns and demands or else prepare for court action. Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. Link Copy link

title: Chinese company sues Govt
text: The Observer A decision taken by a parliamentary committee to suspend operations of Blue Wave Beverages Limited has been challenged in the courts of law. Blue Wave Beverages, the manufacturers of Blue Wave purified water, has dragged the Attorney General and Uganda National Bureau of Standards (UNBS) to court to challenge a decision by Parliament’s committee on Equal Opportunities, chaired by Kampala Central MP, Mohammed Nsereko, to order for its closure. In a suit, filed by WEB Advocates and Solicitors, Quan Liu, the managing director of Blue Wave, the applicant stated that on November 23, 2016, he appeared before the committee following an invitation to interact with MPs on its operations. Liu states in the affidavit that after interacting with the committee, they left Parliament, only to learn later that Nsereko had paraded bottles bearing a brand of Blue Wave from a carton, which he publicly denounced as unfit for human consumption. Liu says that prior to the public denouncement of the product, he was never shown the bottled water to verify that the batch numbers, the bottles and products were from the factory. The affidavit says that on 23rd November 2016, inspectors from Uganda National Bureau of Standards (UNBS) went to the factory, carried out on-site inspection and found the production line and systems compliant. The company was later shocked to receive a letter from UNBS Executive Director Dr Ben Manyindo suspending their production. Blue Wave says the decision to suspend their operations was wrong, in spite of a report issued by UNBS on November 21, 2016, two days before its appearance in Parliament, stating that the company was compliant. The company is seeking damages amounting to Shs 8bn on grounds that it has lost public goodwill and confidence; loss of sales revenue for the days since its closure; cancelled contracts. Justice Mugambe has given the parties two days to hold negotiations out of court and reconvene on Thursday, 22nd December 2016 with a decision. title: Ugandan farmers need agricology experts – new France ambassador
text: The Observer France recently appointed STEPHANIE RIVOAL as their new ambassador to Uganda. Speaking to Ali Twaha on the sidelines of an event, she revealed her country’s development plans for the next couple of years in Uganda, and more. What are some of the key highlights that the French embassy plans to look at in the next couple of years? The three elements we would like to push as a country in Uganda is as much as possible the stability and security in the region. So, we have a military cooperation with the country to train the Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF), who are actually going to Somalia. We have mountain training, which is very specific because we have mountains in France. It’s in both our interest to have a secure country to develop. Sustainable development is our second priority. We have a development agency which is pushing for big projects in hydro electricity, transport, energy, water and sanitation. These are the key projects we will push on sustainable development. And because we are doing water, we very much would like to look at irrigation for agriculture. I feel this country has a huge and enormous potential in agriculture. Our last one is to enhance economic development and relationship between the two countries because French companies have very high expertise in some areas, which I would like to bring in. You seem to emphasize the potential of agriculture. How much can it impact on Uganda’s economy if fully embraced? I am highly interested in agriculture because I spent 11 years in the humanitarian sector. So, I have been to more than 50 countries to address the issue of food insecurity and nutrition. And this is what I have been doing for the last 11 years. I have seen the collateral damage that industrialized, overly-mechanized agriculture with the use of chemicals, fertilizers pesticides has done. I have seen the strategy and I have seen the opposite. So, we are attached to preserving the planet, and there is a way to do agriculture which does all these things. The potential in Uganda is enormous. If there is potential, where do you see the gaps and problems? I think there is lack of knowledge about agricology. It’s highly technical. You need to have people who studied the crops, the soil, the climate, the rain and temperature in order to design an ecosystem with the best combination of crops and animals that can give you the highest production of meat and cereals or coffee or whatever it is. So, if you haven’t studied that, you cannot know it immediately. The local people know a lot about their land but it could be enhanced [for better yields]. So, possibly we could have these people [experts in] agricology to come and talk to them. And we are bringing one [from France]. Then there is the issue of water. Irrigation is not done enough. People seem to wait for the rain. Also, the land is in small pieces. The cooperative model should be pushed here. There used to be more cooperatives. Possibly they can be revived or reorganized because when there is a group of people, then you share everything. Why export coffee to Kenya [for value addition] and then back to Uganda for consumption? This is silly. Uganda should be able to do it all. Should Ugandans passionate about agriculture expect some funding in that regard from the embassy? We can’t do it all. We are only France and our focus has been on transport, energy, hydro electricity and sanitation. I am not going to change the strategy be- cause I am representing France’s interest in Uganda. But as the ambassador, you do have influence over some of these decisions… Yes I do influence but I bring in these experts. They do reports which will be brought to the ministry of agriculture and the ministry of water. So, I am here to make sure the knowledge is shared. In terms of programming and funding, we are not the only ones [offering financial assistance to Uganda]; Europe is funding. So, once you are convinced about a design about agriculture, the money will come from various donors. I just want to make sure that Uganda is protecting its own. How can Uganda make itself more attractive to France in the areas of tourism and trade? The thing is I haven’t been to the national parks but I am going very soon. But this is an amazing country in that respect [tourism]. The thing is the French people don’t know any- thing about Uganda; they know a lot about the French-speaking African countries. They know about Cote d’Ivoire and Senegal. They also know a lot about Kenya which has done a big job at promoting itself in France. Uganda has to do the same. You have to pay advertising on the French TV. The language is an issue but if Kenya made it, why not Uganda? Lastly, if you’re to convince an investor to put his money here, which sector would you recommend? I would say tourism for the French citizen maybe. Some people from France may put up restaurants near the parks, where people can actually speak French. They come for only one week and if they can’t speak very good English, it’s not easy for them. So, you can have that. They can also invest in agriculture and technology. alitwaha9@gmail.com Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. Link Copy link

title: One year later, BATU hits back at tobacco law
text: The Observer With the sale of its products facing a threat as a tough anti-tobacco legislation takes effect, British American Tobacco Uganda has decided to fight back, writes DERRICK KIYONGA. After what it calls a “one year of critically studying” the Tobacco Control Act 2015 (TCA), tobacco giant British American Tobacco Uganda (BATU) has gone to the Constitutional court challenging the constitutionality of that law. In its petition filed on December 16, 2016, BATU asserts that it’s going to demonstrate to the judges that the act, when read as a whole, has the effect of unjustifiably singling out the tobacco industry for discriminative treatment, which amounts to a ban on the right to trade in and or consume a legal product (tobacco and tobacco products). The act was passed into law by parliament on July 28, 2015. President Yoweri Museveni signed it into law on September 19, 2015. BATU has been reducing its presence in Uganda over the last five years. The company first shifted its tobacco processing unit to Kenya, and then later stopped its tobacco growing business. It then sold its warehouse at Old Port Bell and decided to only market its different cigarette brands. High costs of production, unfair competition practices in the leaf-growing business, and new pieces of legislations that the company described as harsh, are some of the reasons as to why BATU has down-sized in Uganda. The backers of the anti-tobacco law rationalised its importance by arguing that, among other things, it was meant to control the demand for consumption of tobacco and its products; promote the health of persons and reduce tobacco- related illnesses and deaths. That said, BATU challenges section 12 of the Act which prohibits smoking in mostly public places. BATU wants Uganda to copy international best practices where hotels, bars and restaurants have designated smoking areas which are properly demarcated and designed with physical planning approvals by relevant government institutions. “This international practice has been developed to comply with the creation of a smoke- free environment for non-smokers within these premises,” the petition reads. According to BATU, section 12(1) of the Act completely prohibits smoking without exception; it contravenes the right to use property for lawful purposes hence being contravention of article 40 (2) of the Constitution. Through Sebalu and Lule advocates, BATU attacks section 12(2) which asks for a 50-meter radius restriction for smoking in outdoor spaces whether it is a designated smoking area or not. The tobacco firm describes the 50-meter radius as “impractical” and will prove to court that it is neither necessary nor appropriate. “[section 12 (2)] creates an effective ban on the right and choice to consume a legal product [tobacco] exercisable by adults,” BATU says, adding that this “contravenes the right to use property for lawful purposes and business or trade by stakeholders like hoteliers, bar operators and restaurant owners, who are able and willing to designate an outdoor space for smoking.” Furthermore, BATU says it contributes significant taxes to the economy, having paid Shs 69bn in 2014 and Shs 71bn in 2015. The Act, BATU adds, could hurt this source of revenue for government. “It constitutes an unnecessary obstacle to trade and is more trade-restrictive than necessary to achieve that stated health objectives of the TCA [Tobacco Control Act],” BATU says, adding that “in effect, curtailing your petitioner’s right to practice a lawful trade, occupation or business, and is therefore in contravention of a guaranteed economic right under article 40(2) of the Constitution.” EMPLOYMENT Also, under attack are sections 25 (3) and 25 (4) of the Act. The section bars individuals who have been involved in any occupational activity with the tobacco industry from being contracted by government in a position where that person is likely to contribute to the formulation and mentoring of public health policies on tobacco control within a period of two years from the end of the engagement with the tobacco industry. BATU takes exception to the section, claiming that no other industry or sector selling potentially-harmful products in Uganda contains the employment restrictions described under sections 25 (3) and 25 (4) of the Act. “Your petitioner contends that the provisions of section 25(3) and 25 (4) of the TCA discriminate against the tobacco sector and are inconsistent with and in contravention of the right to practice a lawful trade, occupation or business…” the petition says. GRAPHIC HEALTH WARNING BATU has a grudge with section 15(2) of the Act which stipulates that the graphic health warning that appears on the unit packet, package or outside packing of a tobacco product shall occupy not less than 65 per cent of the principal display area. The 65 per cent health graphic was an increment from 30 per cent previously described by the Uganda National Bureau of Standards. “Your petitioner contends that section 15(2) has an effect of unreasonably restricting the space available to your petitioner in its practice of a lawful trade, occupation and business, leaving your petitioner with only approximately one third of the pack to display its trademark,” BATU says. MANUFACTURING Section 16(2)(c) which provides that a person shall not import, manufacture distribute, process, sell, offer for sale or bring into the country a smokeless or favoured tobacco product is also under challenge. According to BATU, the Act fails to provide any basis for identifying and measuring what amounts to a “flavoured tobacco product” and thus imposes a vague, uncertain and unreasonable restriction. “Your petitioner contends that the prohibition on all favoured tobacco products distorts fair competition by restricting the ability of companies to compete by way of product differentiation, creates an effective ban on the right and choice to trade in a legal product [tobacco] and deprives your petitioner of its legitimate property rights as your petitioner will be prohibited from selling certain brands, and using trademarks associated with those brands….,” the petition says. dkiyonga@obsever.ug Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. title: Cement industry in huge leaps as public projects push up demand
text: The Observer Huge government projects and construction at- tract top dollar in the cement industry as old players expand while new entrants take a bet, writes ALON MWESIGWA. At Namawojolo, Mukono district, off Jinja-Kampala highway, rising structures dot the skyline. A massive chunk of land – 131 acres – is under development, with graders chipping away the ground while workers place final touches on construction. The sound of the grinding mills can be heard from a distance. This is home to Kampala Cement Limited, the latest addition to Uganda’s cement industry, where the company says it has the capacity to produce more than one million tonnes annually. City lawyer MacDosman Kabega, one of the company owners, told The Observer that they had so far invested 110m euros (Shs 412bn ) in the project, which opened officially in September last year. Less than two years old in operation, Kampala Cement scooped a major deal to supply cement to the 800MW Karuma plant, ahead of older firms such as Hima Cement, which is yet to officially supply cement to the same power plant. In September, it supplied 1,200 tonnes of cement to Karuma. To prop up local content requirements, the Karuma contractors needed a producer of quality cement. They had said that most local producers did not meet the standards. They turned to Kenya, where they got supplies from Savanna Cement Limited. Kampala Cement Managing Director Bob Baryaw said the firm has already had officials from the standard gauge railway test its cement to see whether it meets the quality. Baryaw said they employ 450 people, 29 of these being expatriates. In a brief profile memo, the company says it started operations with a capacity to produce 20,000 tonnes a year. However, company officials said the plant was upgraded to produce one million tonnes per year. Kampala Cement’s factory represents one of the big movers and shakers in the cement industry. As government embarks on major infrastructure projects, cement producers are taking positions to cash in. The market is witnessing strong appetite from new cement players while the older firms expand their production capacities. NEW PLAYERS While the old players are consolidating their positions in the sector, the country is getting appetite for new entrants. Last year, Kenya’s National Cement announced that it was to spend at least $200m to build a new plant in Mbale. It said construction would start by the end of 2016, although it has not started. Also, in 2012 Afghan investors said they had plans to set up a multi-million cement factory in Moroto district. The firm, Moroto Cement (U) Ltd, is expect- ed to produce one million tonnes annually. In October, government announced it would set up a cement factory in Karamoja through a public- private partnership with Moroto Ateker Cement Co Limited. There have been reports that Africa’s richest man Aliko Dangote was also eying the Ugandan market. Some of these pronouncements are yet to materialise. MOVEMENTS In September, Lafarge’s Hima Cement announced it was to spend $40m on a new plant in Tororo Nyakesi, Rubongi sub-county, a small distance from its main rival – Tororo Cement Limited. Rubongi sub-county is one of the areas where Guangzhou Dongsong Energy Group Ltd is expected to mine phosphates and build a $620m fertilizer plant. Hima Cement signed an MOU with Guangzhou to supply it with cement. Daniel Pettersson, the chief executive officer, said then: “We are embarking on several capacity building projects starting with the construction of a grinding station at the end of 2016; we are in final stages of exploration of limestone positions in northeastern Uganda to support clinker position.” In 2010, Hima Cement invested $120 million at its Kasese plant, which saw production capacity move to 900,000 metric tonnes per annum. On completion, the expansion to Tororo expansion will further increase Hima Cement’s capacity to 1.9 million tonnes per year. Hima Cement is also preparing to launch Ready Mix Concrete operations in Kigali, Rwanda, within the first quarter of 2017, which will be followed by similar operations in Uganda. “We are very positive about the long-term prospects of the cement industry in Uganda,” Patterson told reporters in September. Meanwhile, Tororo Cement, the country’s biggest cement manufacturer, last year announced it would spend $25m on plant expansion. It said its capacity would upgrade from 1.8 million tonnes to three million tonnes, maintaining its position as the biggest cement manufacturer in the country. Brij Mohan Gragrani, Tororo Cement’s CEO, said last year: “The expansion is proposed in view of market demand in Uganda and the neighbouring countries.” He said they would construct more cement grinding mills, cement storage silos, rotary packers, and clinker feeding system and clinker sheds. Tororo Cement has also gone to Moroto, where they are expected to put up a new plant. The firm is already supplying cement to Isimba dam. Uganda will become an oil-producing country by 2020/2021, according to government’s target. Combined, the biggest projects in the oil and gas sector – the refinery, pipeline and storage facilities, etc – will cost more than $10bn. Uganda is finishing compensation for the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) and construction could begin later in 2017. The Jinja-bridge construction has also started. Most major roads are undergoing construction, including mega projects such as the Kampala-Entebbe expressway. Parliament has given government a go-ahead to borrow $136m for the Busega-Mpigi expressway, expected to start in 2018. Government has also proposed to build the Kampala-Jinja express- way. CONSTRUCTION Aside from public projects, the real estate sector has been growing, although demand has waned in recent months. For instance, although rental demand has flattened, according to Knight Frank report for 2016, the real estate sector “registered an increase in the number of properties which came onto our books for sale first half of 2016. These properties are mainly in the greater Kampala Metropolitan areas of Kira, Naalya and Najjeera, which are becoming increasingly popular for middle-income home owners.” Many people are taking salary loans to construct houses. Last financial year, the construction sector did not perform well partly as a result of high interest rates. The sector grew by only 0.5 per cent, according to Bank of Uganda figures. Developers, however, are optimistic about the future. The central bank has been easing its key rate, which is expected to give bankers room to cut interest rates. This will boost borrowers’ confidence and spur activity in sectors such as construction. The regional market is also open. In 2015, Uganda exported cement worth $80.13m, a drop from $89m in 2014. RAW MATERIALS Production of limestone, a key raw material in cement production, continues to grow. According to Uganda Bureau of Statistic’s abrastract2015, the production of limestone increased by 18.2 per cent from 922,000 tonnes in 2013 to 1,090,000 tonnes in 2014 and the quantity of Pozzolana increased by 19.1 percent from 623,000 tonnes in 2013 to 742,000 tonnes in 2014. The remaining viable limestone deposits are in the Karamoja sub-region – where many cement companies have rushed to. The exploration process is usually marred by land disputes. Kampala Cement is importing clinker from China, company officials said. In Uganda, they get pozzolana, another main component in cement production, from Kapchorwa in northern Uganda. amwesigwa@observer.ug Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. Link Copy link

title: Chinese firm CCCC aids St Mary’s College Kisubi
text: The Observer China Communications Construction Company has completed the construction of walkways at St Mary’s College Kisubi (SMACK), so as to facilitate a good learning environment. According to Joseph Zheng, the acting country manager of CCCC, they embarked on the project with the aim of improving the education environment in the area they operate in. He noted that CCCC is passionate about improving communities and that they would continue to promote people’s welfare through such projects. Construction of the walkways took 40 days and cost the construction firm Shs 324 million ($90,000). “We decided to build new walkways that were in a sorry state at St Mary’s College [in Wakiso] to ease movement by students as they study and also ensure their safety,” said Zheng at the handover ceremony held at the school campus last week on Tuesday. The SMACK head teacher, Brother Deodati Aganyira, thanked CCCC for its gesture, saying: “After the facelift, the school got a totally-new look and for this we are grateful. On behalf of the school administration, I pledge out total commitment in ensuring that this facility is put to best use for the benefit of the community.” SMACK has a student population of more than 1,360. This is an increase of nearly 70 per cent compared to 20 years ago, and the college has been upgrading its facilities. Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. Link Copy link

title: Higher education council calls for govt support on compliance
text: The Observer The executive director of the National Council for Higher Education (NCHE), Prof John Opuda-Asibo, has called for government support in ensuring that universities and other tertiary institutions follow regulations. Prof Opuda-Asibo said some universities operate under the instructions of courts of law, something that does not make their operations legitimate. “Whereas we may recommend the revoking of an institution’s license, effecting closure is very difficult to implement as those universities tend to run to courts of law. This conflicts with our mandate while regulating higher education,” Opuda-Asibo said during the inauguration of NCHE’s new premises in Kyambogo on Monday. NCHE was established in 2003 as a result of the Universities and Other Tertiary Institutions Act to guide, support and enhance access to relevant quality higher education at both public and private institutions. Dr Alex Kagume, the NCHE deputy executive director, told The Observer that the council was still battling a court case with privately-owned Fairland University, based in Walukuba-Masese zone in Jinja. In March 2013, NCHE revoked Fairland’s license after it failed to meet minimum requirements to be recognised as a fully-fledged university. These included having no staff, infrastructure, or accredited programmes but the university is still operational. “We had refused to give them a license but they went to court and got it through a court order. Court also gave us interim orders to stop us from implementing our duties until the matter is settled,” Kagume said. “This is where we want government to help us to execute our mandate.” According to Opuda-Asibo, the need to enforce compliance is vital since access to higher education has increased form one public university in 1986 to nine, and 47 private universities – 38 on provisional licenses and nine chartered. Today, there are 214 licensed tertiary institutions. “Now, if all these institutions run to courts all the time, how shall we be operating if they don’t follow our guidelines?” he said. Meanwhile, in a speech read for him by vice president Edward Kiwanuka Ssekandi, President Museveni said with a new home, NCHE needs to be more active in shaping the direction and destiny of higher education. “I still emphasize that our education must be made and seen to be relevant. We should continue to invest more in sciences, technology and Engineering which are bedrock disciplines on which we need to anchor our development,” Museveni said. The state minister for higher education, Dr John Muyingo, urged NCHE to only accredit programmes that are relevant and competitive for the labour market both locally and internationally. He said NCHE’s new home would give it a better leverage to perform its mandate as required by the law. The new three-storeyed building, on Kigobe road in Kyambogo, was constructed by China Nanjing Uganda Ltd at a cost of Shs 5.5bn. It comprises of staff offices, a library, data center, 100-seater conference room, printery, boardrooms and restrooms. nangonzi@observer.ug Sign up and get daily updates right to your inbox. title: Praises pour in for Cardinal Wamala at 90
text: The Observer “Life is a gift from God. There is no merit of my own that I am 90 years old. I thank you all for joining me to thank God who has been generous to me by giving me so many years. I reassure your words of love and your gifts. I pray that we continue to remain in love.” These were the simple words the retired archbishop of Kampala archdiocese, Emmanuel Cardinal Wamala, used to appreciate people who turned up to celebrate his 90th birthday on December 16, 2016. In a simple grass compound in Nsambya, a Kampala suburb, guests from all walks of life gathered to pay tribute to a man of God who has spent many decades serving the church and the country. There were many notables: former prime minister Apolo Nsibambi was present, and so was former Democratic Party president-general Paul Kawanga Ssemogerere. Lord mayor Erias Lukwago was there, as well as Masaka district LC-V chairman Jude Mbabaali. Dr Loius Kasekende, the deputy governor of Bank of Uganda, was there too, so was Margaret Nantongo Zziwa, the former speaker of the East African Legislative Assembly. NRM secretary general Justine Kasule Lumumba and many other historical men and women of letters were present. The guest of honour was prime minister Rukahana Rugunda. Born on December 15, 1926 in Bikira parish in Masaka, Wamala attended Kalisizo primary school before joining Bukalasa seminary where he completed his school certificate. From here, he went to Katigondo major seminary and thereafter joined The Pontifical University in Rome, Italy, where he studied philosophy, according to a book about him authored by Robert Ssempa and launched on the same day. Cardinal Wamala was ordained priest in Rome in December 1957, and later named by Pope John Paul II as the founding bishop of Kiyinda Mityana in 1958. He later became archbishop of Kampala archdiocese, replacing the late Emmanuel Cardinal Nsubuga. When Cardinal Wamala arrived at the venue for his birthday celebrations, accompanied by VIP guests, everyone stood up, clapping. In unison, the guests started singing: “Happy birthday to you x2. Happy birthday dear Cardinal…” Speaker after speaker described Cardinal Wamala as a humble and forthright man who has played an important role in shaping the church in Uganda. Prime minister Rugunda described Cardinal Wamala as a man whose humility and sincerity is a lesson for everyone to emulate. He saluted Cardinal Wamala for nurturing people in both the church and the political arena. Pointing out some lady politicians such as the late Bernadette Bigirwa, former Woman MP for Bushenyi, and Mbarara Municipality and now Oxfam executive director Winnie Byanyima, former Kamuli district chairperson Salaamu Musumba and current NRM secretary general Kasule Lumumba, Rugunda said Cardinal Wamala’s mentorship of these ladies is a powerful example of great leadership. These lady politicians are mentioned in the cardinal’s book. Dr Rugunda then spoke about the political views of Cardinal Wamala. “Cardinal Wamala does not normally comment on political issues, but when he does, he is sober, and speaks in a manner that is clear, with immense wisdom,” Rugunda said amidst nods of approval from the audience. “We salute you for your clarity, candor and humility. When he speaks, whether you agree with him or not, you cannot ignore him. Thank you for being straightforward. Thank you for your work for the people of Uganda irrespective of their various affiliations.” Rugunda concluded his remarks by asking Robert Ssempa, the author of the book: Emmanuel Cardinal Wamala—A man of Humility and Love for All, to read a portion on page 53. And it goes like this: “There was a time His Grace, Archbishop Paul Bakyenga of Mbarara shared with me [the author] how he fancied the qualities of Emmanuel Cardinal Wamala. He is not divisive. He respects everyone and values the dignity of every person. Always cautious about what people said of others, Cardinal Wamala would approach individuals with fatherly concern and fraternal charity. In a way, he curtailed rumors about persons. He discouraged mudslinging and character assassinations, on which some people rely in attempts to win themselves over, but cheap popularity.” After all the speeches, there was a feast of all tribes of foods and drinks. It was a Friday evening to remember and a first for me – celebrating the birthday of a cardinal who was turning 90 years. julius.mucunguzi@gmail.com The author is a communications advisor to the prime minister.
